attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post. Not a quotation of anyone else.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both clauses and the 'especially' emphasis. The connectivity clause is close to rhetoric. The testable core is the firm claim that LLMs are extremely bad at deterministic workplace actions.

contract.note: The plain reading (broadly unreliable at rule-bound workplace actions given natural-language instructions) is ordinary and fair. There is no failure threshold, the task population is undefined, and the evaluator chose the Q1 2026 period, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Versioned APEX-Agents preprint from January 2026. Across 480 professional cross-application tasks, the best Pass@1 was 24%, showing frequent failure. These tasks are reasoning-heavy and not representative of routine actions.

Independent METR report (published May 2026, before the cutoff) assessing February–March systems. It finds very strong performance on checkable technical tasks, which undercuts a blanket 'extremely bad'. It does not show broad office-workflow reliability.
Vendor announcement quoting a customer's 94% result on an insurance benchmark. No public methodology. Company disclosure only.

reviews.rationale: Part holds: a reproducible benchmark shows agents failing most demanding professional workflows (best Pass@1 24%). Part does not: METR shows agents performing strongly on checkable, rule-bound technical tasks, against a blanket 'extremely bad'. Neither side covers a representative population of deterministic workplace actions, so the evidence splits by domain.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the three figures, their dates and 'no way to reconcile'. 'If that's the case' points back to his revenue-mix estimate and does not condition the incompatibility claim.

contract.note: Testing whether the reported figures can coexist, with their original qualifications kept, is a fair reading of 'reconcile'. The result turns on reading the $5B as the lower bound the source stated, which Zitron left out.

evidence.note: Sworn CFO declaration filed March 9, 2026. The context shows lifetime revenue 'exceeding $5 billion to date', a lower bound only. The quoted sentence is the next line, as the locator says. The relevant text is visible in the context.
Anthropic's own February 12 disclosure of a $14B run rate. That is an annualized measure, not realized revenue. Company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The lifetime figure was reported as exceeding $5B, with no upper bound. Even accepting the unverified $4.5B for 2025, adding pre-2025 revenue and 2026 revenue at a $14B run rate gives a lifetime total above $5B, which fits the lower bound. Since the reported figures can coexist, the claimed incompatibility fails.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The quoted phrase is Nscale's marketing, cited as his example.

semantics.note: The proposition drops the 'pile of scaffolding' detail and the $2B fundraising clause, both of which the speaker asserted and the contract tests. 'Seem to' is an appearance framing, not a probability hedge, so the claim is still a firm observation.

contract.note: Reading 'don't exist' as little or no physical development is fair and ordinary. Without a denominator for 'a lot', the prevalence part depends on interpretation and on representative data.

evidence.note: Guardian firsthand visit in February 2026, published March 9. The Loughton site was still a working scaffolding yard months before its due date. This supports the Nscale example only.
Nscale's own March 9 announcement of a $2B Series C. It matches the stated raise but is a company disclosure, and its closing basis is unspecified.

reviews.rationale: What holds: the Nscale site had no visible development and was a scaffolding yard in Q1 2026. Nscale also announced a $2B raise, though only by company disclosure. What is not established: the main claim that a lot of AI data center projects don't exist. No representative inventory is in the packet, and one example cannot show prevalence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary of his argument in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully condenses the claims of cherry-picking, launch-boosted four-week API windows and annualization.

contract.note: Requiring actual selective choice of favorable windows or reporting dates is the ordinary meaning of 'cherry-picking'. Merely using a trailing formula would not count, and the contract says so fairly.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own April 6 disclosure of a run rate above $30B. It gives no underlying windows, alternative windows, or reasons for the reporting dates. Company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The packet confirms only that a run-rate announcement fell in the period. It has no API revenue series, no alternative windows and no evidence of why the reporting dates were chosen. So the evidence neither shows selective window choice nor rules it out.
